tips.title: Count the notes against the syllables
tips.body: That is the whole test for word setting. One note to a syllable is **syllabic**; a group of notes on a single syllable is a **melisma**. You do not have to judge anything — you count, and the answer falls out.

tips.title: Name the voice, not the person
tips.body: **Soprano, mezzo-soprano, alto, countertenor, tenor, baritone, bass.** A mark scheme wants the voice type. "A woman singing" and "a high voice" are both weaker than *soprano*, and a countertenor is a high male voice that people routinely mistake for a woman.

tips.title: Strophic or through-composed?
tips.body: Does each verse get the **same** music? Then it is **strophic** — the commonest shape for a folk song, a hymn or a ballad. Does the music keep changing as the words do? Then it is **through-composed**. One question, two words, and it answers most structure questions about song.

tips.title: Word painting needs the word
tips.body: You cannot discuss word painting without quoting the word. *Rising notes on "ascending"*, *a falling line on "drop"*, *a long note on "eternal"* — the word and the device together, or the point cannot be credited.

tips.title: SATB, with a mezzo and a baritone in the gaps
tips.body: Choir order runs **S**oprano, **A**lto, **T**enor, **B**ass, top to bottom. Slot the **mezzo** between soprano and alto and the **baritone** between tenor and bass, and remember the **countertenor** is a man singing in the alto range.

why.matters: Every question about vocal music starts with the same thing: what kind of voice is that? Seven names cover almost everything, and the two that catch people out, the countertenor and the mezzo, catch people out because the ranges overlap. After the voice come the words: whether each syllable gets one note or twenty, whether the music paints what the words mean, and where the line sits in the voice's range. Those are the mechanisms behind every effect a singer makes, and naming them is what an answer needs instead of *she sings very high*.

examples.title: The man who gets written down as a soprano
examples.body: A countertenor is a male voice singing in the alto range, usually in falsetto, and plenty of students hear one and write *soprano*. The mistake is understandable, because neighbouring voice types overlap by design: each spans about two octaves and sits a little below the last, which is why a four-part choir can sing a chord close together. From the bottom of a bass to the top of a soprano is about 3.4 octaves, and every voice you will name sits somewhere in that stack.

examples.title: One note a syllable, or twenty
examples.body: A hymn gives each syllable one note, because a crowd has to sing it and the words have to be heard. A gospel singer puts twenty notes on one syllable, because the display is the point and the words were understood the first time. Syllabic and melismatic are not styles; they are decisions about what the moment is for. Purcell does both in one aria: speech rhythms for most of the text, then a long melisma on *eternal* that seems to go on forever, which is the meaning of the word made audible.

examples.title: The singer who sounds strained without a high note
examples.body: Range is the distance between a part's lowest and highest notes. Tessitura is where it mostly sits. A line that touches a high note once and lives comfortably in the middle has a wide range and an easy tessitura; a line that never leaves the top of the stave has a high tessitura and sounds strained even without an extreme note in it. Saying which one is producing the effect is a grade 9 observation, because it explains what *she sings very high* only describes.

steps.title: The voices
steps.body:
Every exam question about vocal music starts with the same thing: **what kind of voice is that?** Seven names cover almost everything.

- **Soprano**
- **Mezzo-soprano**
- **Alto**
- **Countertenor**
- **Tenor**
- **Baritone**
- **Bass**

Each spans roughly **two octaves**, and neighbouring types **overlap**, which is why a four-part chord can be sung close together rather than spread out. From the lowest note of a bass to the highest of a soprano is about **3.4 octaves**.

**Two that catch people out.**

A **countertenor** is a **male** voice singing in the alto range, usually in **falsetto**. Plenty of students hear one and write "soprano". It is common in Baroque and earlier music, and a rise in the popularity of that repertoire has brought it back.

A **mezzo-soprano** sits between soprano and alto. If a female voice sounds warm and full rather than bright and high, mezzo is likelier than soprano.

**Range is not the same as tessitura.** The **range** is the distance between a part's lowest and highest notes. The **tessitura** is where the part mostly sits. A soprano line that touches a high C once but lives around the middle of the stave has a wide range and a comfortable tessitura; a line that never leaves the top of the stave has a **high tessitura** and sounds strained even without an extreme note in it. Saying so is a grade 9 observation, because it explains an effect that "she sings very high" does not.

**Choirs** are usually **SATB**: Soprano, Alto, Tenor, Bass. Four parts, top to bottom. **A cappella** means singing with no accompaniment at all.

boxes.body: A male voice singing above its usual range in a lighter tone. What a countertenor mostly uses.

boxes.body: Voices with no accompaniment at all. Not the same as unison, and not the same as solo.

steps.title: Setting words to music
steps.body:
A composer with a text has to decide how many notes each syllable gets. That decision is **word setting**, and it is one of the most asked-about things in this area of study.

**Syllabic.** One note to each syllable. The words come through clearly, so syllabic setting suits narrative — a story, a verse, a recitative, a rap. Nothing is in the way of the text.

**Melismatic.** A group of notes on one syllable — a **melisma**. The words slow almost to a halt and the voice becomes an instrument. Melisma is used for emphasis, for display, and for the emotional high point of a piece, which is why it turns up on the title word of a chorus and on the important word of a Baroque aria alike.

The test is arithmetic. **Count the notes against the syllables.** Equal numbers is syllabic; more notes than syllables is melismatic.

**Word painting** is different and more specific: the music **illustrates** what the word means. Rising notes on *ascending*. A falling line on *drop*. A long held note on *eternal*. A trill on *trembling*. It is a composer deliberately illustrating a word or phrase with a matching musical image.

> Purcell's *Music for a While* sets the word **drop** nine times over, on weak off-beats in a descending pattern, depicting the snakes dropping from Alecto's head.

That is a complete word-painting point: the device, the word, and what it depicts. Without the word it is not a point at all.

**Text setting also has to respect stress.** English words have stressed and unstressed syllables, and a setting that puts a long note on an unstressed one sounds wrong however good the tune is. Listening for whether the musical stress matches the spoken stress is a genuinely advanced observation.

visuals.alt: A table showing how counting notes against syllables decides whether a setting is syllabic or melismatic

visuals.problem: A singer takes eleven notes over the single syllable "love". Describe the setting and what it is for.

steps.text: Eleven notes, one syllable, so the setting is melismatic.
steps.note: melismatic: more notes than syllables. The count decides it, not the impression.

steps.text: The group of notes on that one syllable is a melisma.
steps.note: Eleven notes long, which is worth saying — a number is evidence.

steps.text: The word almost stops while the voice keeps moving.
steps.note: That is the effect: the text pauses and the music takes over.

steps.text: So it marks the word as the emotional centre of the phrase.
steps.note: Which is why melisma lands on the title word of a chorus and on the key word of an aria.

check.prompt: A singer takes nine notes over one syllable of a word. Give the term for that group of notes.
check.solution: A **melisma**: a group of notes used to set just one syllable of text. The adjective is *melismatic*. One note per syllable is **syllabic** writing, and the contrast between the two within a single song is usually worth pointing out.

steps.title: The shapes songs take
steps.body:
Four shapes cover most vocal music, and you can tell them apart by listening for what returns.

**Strophic.** The **same music for every stanza** of the text. Hymns, folk songs, ballads and carols are usually strophic. It is the simplest shape and it puts all the variety in the words.

**Through-composed.** **Different music** for some or all of the stanzas, so the music follows the story rather than repeating under it. It is the alternative to strophic, and it suits a text whose mood changes.

**Verse and chorus.** The verses change their words and keep their music; the **chorus** returns with its words unchanged. This is the shape of most popular song, including *Killer Queen*. It is not the same as strophic: in the strict sense a strophic song has no separate chorus (a short refrain after each verse is the most it has).

**Ternary, or the da capo aria.** A B A: an opening section, a contrasting middle, then the opening again — usually decorated on its return. It became the standard late-Baroque operatic aria shape, and Purcell's *Music for a While* anticipates it, with the opening material returning at bar 29 in identical form with a slight extension.

**And two words for how the voice enters the drama.**

**Recitative** is sung speech: syllabic, following the natural rhythm of the words, lightly accompanied, used to carry the story forward.

**Aria** is the song proper: melodic, often melismatic, where the character stops and feels something. The pattern *recitative, then aria* runs through opera, oratorio and cantata alike.

Around these sit **intro**, **pre-chorus**, **middle eight** or **bridge**, **instrumental**, **outro** — the sections of a popular song — and a **refrain**, which is a line or two returning at the end of every verse without being a full chorus.

steps.title: What is underneath the voice
steps.body:
Half of any vocal texture is the accompaniment, and an answer that only describes the singing has described half the music.

**A cappella.** Nothing at all. Voices alone, whether one or a hundred. A solo unaccompanied line is **monophonic**; four voices in harmony are **homophonic**.

**Continuo.** A bass line with a harpsichord, organ or lute filling in the chords. The Baroque standard, and hearing one points strongly to the Baroque. Purcell's ground bass is played by the harpsichord left hand and doubled by a bass viol.

**Piano.** The nineteenth-century art song, where the piano is an equal partner rather than a support, often depicting something the words only describe.

**Orchestra.** Opera, oratorio and musical theatre. The orchestra has to leave room for the words, so its textures under singing are typically **melody-dominated homophony** rather than counterpoint.

**Band.** Drums, bass, guitar and keyboard: the popular song. And with it, **the studio**, which is an accompaniment of its own kind. Since the 1960s a single singer can be **multi-tracked** into a whole harmony section, **double tracked** to thicken one line, given **reverb** to place them in a space that does not exist, or corrected in pitch. Some of what you hear in a popular vocal was never sung in one take by one person, and saying so is part of describing the sonority.

**Vocal techniques worth naming**: **vibrato**, the slight wobble in pitch that warms a held note; **falsetto**, a male voice singing light and high; **belting**, singing loudly in a chest voice high in the range, characteristic of musical theatre; **scat**, wordless improvised jazz singing; **portamento**, a slide between notes that a voice can make and a piano cannot; **ad libs**, free decoration usually over a fade; and **rap**, rhythmic speech over a beat.

steps.title: Sacred, secular, and what language
steps.body:
Two questions place a piece of vocal music in its world almost immediately.

**Is it sacred or secular?** Sacred music is for worship; secular music is everything else. For centuries the church was the largest employer of musicians in Europe, which is why so much surviving early vocal music is sacred.

**What language is it in?** Latin usually points to church music, especially before about 1600. A **vernacular** language — the everyday language of the place — points to secular music, or to church music after the Reformation, when services began to be held in local languages.

That gives you a rough map of vocal genres.

**Sacred.** **Plainchant**: a single unaccompanied line, Latin, modal, no regular beat, monophonic however many sing it. **Mass** and **motet** in the Renaissance, polyphonic and imitative. **Oratorio** and **cantata** in the Baroque, with soloists, choir and orchestra — a cantata is a work in several movements for singers and instruments, particularly associated with the Baroque, and it can be sacred or secular.

**Secular.** The **madrigal**, a Renaissance part-song, usually secular, often with word painting. **Opera** from around 1600. The **art song** or **lied**, for voice and piano. **Musical theatre**, which brings together songs, spoken dialogue, acting and dance in a popular idiom. **Folk song**, passed on by **oral tradition** — learnt by listening and repeating rather than from notation. And **popular song** in all its forms.

**What this is for.** The unfamiliar extract in Section A is closely related to a set work. Placing it — sacred or secular, what language, what accompaniment, what century — tells you which vocabulary to reach for before you have said anything about the music at all.

steps.title: Two songs, nearly three centuries apart
steps.body:
The two Vocal Music set works are about three hundred years apart, and the same vocabulary describes both. Here is how.

**Purcell, *Music for a While*.** A Baroque song for voice and **continuo** — in the edition studied, soprano with harpsichord and bass viol. It is built on a **ground bass**: a **3-bar** pattern, entirely in quavers and arpeggio based, repeating while the voice above it changes. The vocal writing mixes **syllabic** and **melismatic** setting, and it is full of **word painting** — most famously on *drop*, sung nine times over on weak off-beats in a descending pattern to depict the snakes dropping from Alecto's head. The opening material returns near the end, which anticipates the **ternary da capo aria**.

**Queen, *Killer Queen*, 1974.** A popular song in **verse and chorus** form, with an instrumental after the first chorus, a guitar solo before the third verse, and an outro that fades. It is in 12/8 with a **swung** feel, and every verse and chorus begins with an **anacrusis**. Its vocal sonority is a studio creation: layered, multi-tracked harmonies that no group of people could produce live.

**What the two share.** A voice over an accompaniment. Words that are set syllabically in the narrative parts and more freely at the emotional ones. A structure built on something returning. And in both, the accompaniment is doing at least as much work as the melody.

**Where they differ.** Purcell's accompaniment is a **fixed bass** with a **realised** keyboard part — improvised from figures by the player in Purcell's day, and written out in the edition studied. Queen's is **constructed in a studio** and is fixed in a completely different sense: it is exactly what was recorded and could not be improvised at all.

Comparing two pieces element by element like this is the skill Section B asks for, where a set work is set against an unfamiliar piece from the same area of study, and you will meet it properly in Year 11.

steps.title: Your turn: place three vocal extracts
steps.body:
Three extracts, described. For each, say **what kind of voice**, **how the words are set**, **what the form is**, and **roughly when or where it comes from** — with a reason for each.

**A.** A solo female voice with a harpsichord and a bass instrument. The bass plays the same four-bar phrase over and over while the voice above it changes continuously. The words are in English. On the word *falling* the voice descends through eight notes.

**B.** Around forty singers, no instruments, all singing the same single line, in Latin, with no beat you could tap.

**C.** One female voice with a band. Verses of one note per syllable, a chorus where the title word is stretched over twelve notes, and behind the chorus three more vocal lines in harmony that are clearly the same singer recorded several times.

Write four short answers for each, then check yourself.

steps.title: Going deeper: writing about a voice
steps.body:
The gap between a middle answer and a top one here is almost entirely **precision**.

| Weak | Strong |
| --- | --- |
| A woman singing | A soprano, with a high tessitura through the chorus |
| She holds a long note | An eleven-note melisma on the title word |
| The words fit the music well | Syllabic in the verse and melismatic in the chorus |
| There is word painting | Eight descending notes on "falling" |
| Lots of backing vocals | Three-part harmony, multi-tracked by the same singer |
| It is quite an old song | A continuo accompanies it, so it is Baroque |
| The singer sounds emotional | Vibrato widens on the held notes, and there is a portamento into the final phrase |

**Four habits.**

**Count, do not judge.** Notes against syllables decides syllabic or melismatic. Nothing about that is a matter of taste.

**Quote the word.** Word painting is a claim about a specific word, so the word has to be in the sentence.

**Describe the accompaniment.** It is half the music and it usually tells you the period.

**Use the tradition's own vocabulary.** *Melisma* and *word painting* and *continuo* for Purcell; *multi-tracking*, *overdubbing* and *falsetto* for Queen. Using Baroque vocabulary for a pop song, or the reverse, reads as not having placed the extract at all.

And one thing that separates the very best answers: **say what the setting does to the words**. Syllabic writing lets a text be understood; melisma stops the text and turns the voice into an instrument. A composer choosing between them is choosing whether the audience should be following the story or feeling something, and saying that is a judgement supported by an observation.

steps.title: What to carry forward
steps.body:
- **Voice types**: Soprano, Mezzo-soprano, Alto, Countertenor, Tenor, Baritone, Bass. A **countertenor** is male. A choir is usually **SATB**.
- **Range** is lowest to highest; **tessitura** is where a part mostly sits. A high tessitura strains even with no extreme note.
- **Word setting**: count notes against syllables. Equal is **syllabic**; more notes than syllables is **melismatic**, and the group on one syllable is a **melisma**.
- **Word painting** illustrates the meaning of a specific word. Quote the word or it is not a point.
- **Forms**: **strophic** repeats the music each stanza; **through-composed** does not; **verse and chorus** returns the chorus with its words; **ternary** or the **da capo aria** is A B A.
- **Recitative** is sung speech carrying the story; an **aria** is where the character stops and feels.
- **Accompaniment**: **a cappella**, **continuo** (Baroque), piano (art song), orchestra, band, and **the studio**.
- **Techniques**: vibrato, falsetto, belting, scat, portamento, ad libs, rap, **multi-tracking** and **double tracking**.
- **Sacred or secular**, and **Latin or vernacular**, place a piece before you have described a note.
- The set works are Purcell's *Music for a While*, on a **3-bar ground bass**, and Queen's *Killer Queen*, **1974**.

The voice must be a countertenor rather than a soprano
The song is sacred rather than secular in its subject
questions.skill: placing a song in its world
questions.solution: A bass line plus a chord-playing instrument realising the harmony is the **continuo**, and it fades out of most music after about 1750. It says nothing at all about the voice type or the subject matter; an art song would be voice and piano.

markScheme.description: a continuo, so Baroque

questions.prompt: Give the term for sung speech, set syllabically and lightly accompanied, used in opera and oratorio to carry the story forward.
questions.solution: **Recitative**. It follows the natural rhythm of the words rather than a tune, so the plot can move quickly. It is usually followed by an **aria**, where the action stops and the character expresses something — the pattern runs through opera, oratorio and cantata alike.

markScheme.description: recitative

questions.prompt: Three harmony lines behind a lead vocal are audibly the same singer. How was that done, and what does it tell you?
options: Multi-tracking, so the recording postdates that technique
A vocal harmoniser, so the harmony was never sung at all
A choir was hired, so the recording must be expensive
Nothing can be told from it, since singers often sound alike
questions.solution: One singer appearing as four is **multi-tracking**: each line recorded separately and laid over the others. It cannot be done live, so it dates the recording after the technique existed, and it is part of the **sonority** — some of what is heard was never sung in one take.

markScheme.description: multi-tracking

questions.prompt: Which pair of features would place an extract as plainchant?
options: Monophonic and modal, in Latin, with no regular pulse
Polyphonic and imitative, in Latin, with a continuo
Homophonic and diatonic, in English, with an organ
Melismatic and chromatic, in Italian, with an orchestra
questions.skill: placing a song in its world
questions.solution: **Plainchant** is a single melodic line — **monophonic** however many are singing it — in Latin, **modal** rather than in a major or minor key, and without a regular beat. Polyphony with a continuo is Baroque; the other two describe later music entirely.

markScheme.description: monophonic, modal, Latin, no regular pulse

questions.prompt: Put these steps in order to make a complete point about the word setting of a vocal extract.
items: Count the notes against the syllables in the phrase
Decide from the count whether the setting is syllabic or melismatic
Find the word where the setting changes, and quote it
Say what that change of setting does to the word's meaning
questions.solution: Each step needs the one before it. The count comes first, because syllabic and melismatic are decided by counting rather than by impression, and the count then decides the setting. Only once you know the setting can you find the word where it changes, and the word has to be quoted for the point to be credited. What the change does to the meaning comes last, because it is a judgement resting on the observations before it.

markScheme.description: the count before the decision
the word found and quoted before its effect
the judgement about meaning last

questions.prompt: Why might a composer set a narrative passage syllabically and a reflective one melismatically?
options: Syllabic setting lets the words be followed; melisma stops the text and lets the voice express
Syllabic setting is easier to sing, so it is used for the longer sections of a work
Melismatic setting uses fewer notes, so it suits the quieter parts of a piece
The two are interchangeable, and composers alternate them to provide variety
questions.solution: The choice is about what the audience should be doing. **Syllabic** writing puts nothing between the listener and the words, so it suits a story. **Melisma** almost stops the text while the voice keeps moving, so it suits a moment of feeling. Melisma uses *more* notes, not fewer, and the two are not interchangeable.

markScheme.description: syllabic for the words, melismatic for expression

questions.prompt: Which claim about word painting is complete enough to be credited?
options: There is a lot of word painting throughout this whole extract
The composer uses word painting to make the words more vivid
The melody rises and falls in a way that matches the text well
Eight descending notes on the word "falling" depict the fall
questions.solution: Word painting is a claim about a **particular word**, so the word has to be quoted and the device named. The other three assert that painting is happening without ever identifying a single instance, so there is nothing for a mark scheme to credit.

markScheme.description: the option quoting the word and naming the device

questions.prompt: A line of text has 14 syllables. The singer uses 14 notes for all of them except one, which is given a melisma of 9 notes. How many notes does the singer sing in total?
questions.solution: Thirteen syllables take one note each, which is 13. The fourteenth takes a melisma of 9. So the total is 13 plus 9, which is **22** notes. Counting like this is exactly how syllabic and melismatic writing are told apart: 22 notes for 14 syllables is melismatic.

questions.prompt:
A vocal extract is played several times, with a skeleton score showing the vocal line.

**On the page:** one flat in the key signature; four crotchets in a bar; a slow tempo. The words are in English.

**What you hear:**

- A solo female voice in a high range, accompanied by a bass instrument and a harpsichord filling in the chords above it.
- The bass plays the same four-bar phrase eleven times without a break; the vocal line above it is different every time.
- Most of the text is set one note to a syllable.
- On the word "weeping" the voice descends through seven notes on that single syllable.
- On the word "endless" the voice holds one note for three bars.
- The music of the opening returns near the end, in the same form with a short extension.

Describe this extract, referring to the voice, the accompaniment, the word setting and the structure, and say roughly when it was written and why.
questions.skill: placing a song in its world
questions.solution:
**Voice and accompaniment.** A solo female voice in a high range is a **soprano**. Underneath it, a bass instrument plays the bass line and a harpsichord fills in the chords above it: that combination is a **continuo**, the defining accompaniment of Baroque vocal music. The harpsichord part would have been **realised** from figures by the player rather than written out in full, which is itself a Baroque practice.

**Structure.** The bass plays the same four-bar phrase **eleven times** without a break while the vocal line above it is different every time. That is a **ground bass** — a repeating phrase in the bass, a common Baroque device of which Purcell is regarded as a master. It is a form built on something fixed with something changing above it, and it gives the music continuous forward motion because the pattern comes round every few seconds. The return of the opening material near the end, in the same form with a short extension, anticipates the **ternary da capo aria** that became standard in later Baroque opera.

**Word setting.** Most of the text is set **one note to a syllable**, which is **syllabic** writing: nothing stands between the listener and the words, so the sense carries. Against that, two moments are quite different.

On **"weeping"** the voice descends through **seven notes on one syllable**. That is a **melisma** — more notes than syllables, so **melismatic** setting — and because the line *falls* on a word about grief it is also **word painting**: the composer illustrates the meaning with a matching musical image.

On **"endless"** the voice holds a single note for **three bars**. Again word painting, and by a different means: a note that will not stop depicts something that does not end. Quoting the word in each case is what makes these points creditable; "there is word painting in it" would not be.

**Date.** The extract is **Baroque**, before about 1750. The continuo is the decisive evidence: it is present in almost all Baroque vocal music and rare afterwards. The ground bass and the extensive word painting both support it, and the English words point to a secular song, or to English church music after the Reformation, rather than Latin chant.

**Overall.** Everything agrees. A soprano over a continuo, a ground bass repeating eleven times, syllabic writing broken by two carefully placed melismas that both paint their words, and a reprise of the opening. Nothing in the extract points to any other period.

questions.prompt:
A vocal extract is played several times, with a skeleton score showing the vocal line and chord symbols above it.

**On the page:** no sharps or flats; four crotchets in a bar. The chord symbols for bars 17 to 24 read C | Am | F | G7, repeating.

**What you hear:**

- Bars 1 to 16: one female voice with an acoustic guitar, one note to each syllable, the melody staying inside a fifth.
- Bars 17 to 24: drums and bass enter; the title word is stretched over twelve notes; behind the voice, three further vocal lines in harmony are audibly the same singer.
- The lead vocal in these bars has been recorded twice and the takes laid over each other.
- Bars 25 to 32: an instrumental, then bars 17 to 24 again.
- The last section repeats the final line of the chorus with free decoration over the top, and the track gets quieter until it disappears.

Describe this extract, referring to the voice and the studio, the word setting, the harmony and the structure.
questions.solution:
**Voice and studio.** A single female voice carries the verse over an acoustic guitar. From bar 17 the sonority changes completely, and both changes are studio work rather than performance. The three harmony lines behind the chorus are **audibly the same singer**, so they were **multi-tracked**: each recorded separately and laid over the others, which no one can do live. The lead vocal itself has been **double tracked** — recorded twice and the takes played together — which thickens it and slightly blurs it, because two takes are never identical. Describing the sonority of this extract without mentioning either would miss half of what makes it sound the way it does.

**Word setting.** The verse is **syllabic**, one note to each syllable, and the melody stays inside a **fifth**, so it is narrow and conversational and the words come through clearly. The chorus does the opposite: the title word is stretched over **twelve notes**, which is a **melisma**. Setting a narrow syllabic verse against a melismatic chorus is one common way a popular song marks the arrival of its hook, and the contrast is what makes the chorus sound like a release rather than simply a louder verse.

**Harmony.** The loop starts on C and uses only chords of C major, so the key is most likely **C major**, and the printed chorus chords read as **I, vi, IV, V7** — C, A minor, F, G7. Three major chords and one minor, which is why the progression can sound bright and wistful at the same time. It **repeats unchanged** through the chorus, so the harmony asks for no attention and all the interest sits in the voice and the production. That is a deliberate choice, not a limitation.

**Structure.** **Verse and chorus** form: a verse in bars 1 to 16, a chorus in bars 17 to 24, an instrumental in bars 25 to 32, and then the chorus again. The final section repeats the last line of the chorus with free decoration over the top — **ad libs** — and the track ends with a **fade**, getting quieter until it disappears rather than stopping. A fade is a mixing-desk ending and cannot be performed live either.

**Overall.** The extract divides cleanly at bar 17, and every element changes there at once: forces, texture, word setting and dynamic. Underneath, a four-chord loop holds still for the whole chorus so that nothing competes with the voice. Three of the features described — the multi-tracked harmony, the double-tracked lead and the fade — exist only because the song was made in a studio, which points to the 1960s or later.

questions.prompt: Which is the difference between strophic form and verse-and-chorus form?
options: A strophic song changes its music for every verse it contains
A strophic song is always sacred and verse and chorus always secular
A strophic song has no chorus; every stanza takes the same music
There is no difference; the two terms mean exactly the same thing
questions.solution: **Strophic** means the same music for every stanza, with no separate returning section. **Verse and chorus** adds a chorus whose *words* come back unchanged. Calling a verse-and-chorus pop song strophic is a common slip, and the two are genuinely different shapes.

markScheme.description: strophic has no chorus; the same music serves every stanza

questions.prompt: Which observation about a vocal line shows the most advanced listening?
options: The tessitura sits high through the chorus, so the singer sounds strained
The singer reaches a very high note at the climax of the chorus
There are several long notes in the chorus of this particular song
The chorus is sung much more loudly than the verse before it
questions.solution: **Tessitura** — where the line mostly sits — explains a quality of sound that a single high note does not. A part that lives at the top strains throughout even with no extreme note in it, and hearing that is a different and harder observation from noticing a peak, a long note or a change of dynamic.

markScheme.description: the option using tessitura to explain the sound

questions.prompt: Compare how a composer of a Baroque song and a producer of a modern popular song each shape a voice, referring to word setting, accompaniment and the resources available to each.
questions.skill: placing a song in its world
questions.solution:
**What they share.** Both work with the same basic decision: how many notes each syllable gets. Both use **syllabic** writing where the words have to be followed and **melisma** where the voice should take over from the text. And in both, the accompaniment does at least as much work as the melody.

**Word setting.** The Baroque composer uses melisma for **word painting**: the notes illustrate the meaning of a particular word, so a falling line lands on *weeping* and a held note on *endless*. The choice is driven by the text word by word. The popular producer uses melisma differently — it lands on the **title word of the chorus**, and its job is to mark the hook rather than to depict anything. Both are using the same technique; one is serving the meaning of a word and the other is serving the shape of the song.

**Accompaniment.** The Baroque song has a **continuo**: a bass instrument and a harpsichord, with the keyboard part **realised** from figures by the player. That means the accompaniment is partly improvised and different at every performance, and it is the reason a ground bass can support a whole song without becoming dull — what sits above it is never quite the same twice. The popular song has a **band** and, just as importantly, **a studio**. Its accompaniment is fixed in the opposite sense: it is exactly what was recorded and cannot vary at all.

**Resources.** This is the real difference. The Baroque composer has however many people are in the room and no way of capturing anything. The producer can **multi-track** one singer into a three-part harmony section, **double track** the lead to thicken it, place the voice in an artificial acoustic with **reverb**, and end the song with a **fade** — none of which can be done live by anybody. So the popular song can present a sonority that has never existed as a performance, while the Baroque song can only ever present one that has.

**What each is trying to achieve.** Purcell's kind of song is written to be **performed**, and every choice assumes a room and a player who will make decisions. Its variety comes from what the performers do above a fixed bass. The modern popular record is made to be **reproduced**: it is a fixed object, identical every time it is played, and its variety comes from what was built into it in the studio. The Baroque composer writes a frame for other people to fill; the producer builds the finished thing.

That is why the same vocabulary — syllabic, melismatic, homophonic, hook, melisma — describes both, and why the answers it produces are so different. The technique is shared; the conditions are not.

examTechnique.body:
**Vocal Music is Area of Study 2**, and its set works are Queen's *Killer Queen* (**1974**) and Purcell's *Music for a While*. Nearly three hundred years separate them, so the vocabulary has to work for both.

**Name the voice type.** Soprano, mezzo-soprano, alto, countertenor, tenor, baritone, bass. And say what it is doing: solo, in harmony, doubled, multi-tracked.

**Say how the words are set.** Syllabic or melismatic, and where each happens. A verse that is syllabic and a chorus that is melismatic is a real observation about a real song.

**Quote the word for word painting.** The device and the word, together.

**Name the form.** Strophic, through-composed, verse and chorus, or a da capo aria. Count the return of the words to decide.

**Say what accompanies the voice.** A continuo, a piano, a band, an orchestra, or nothing at all — **a cappella**.

**Vocal techniques have names.** Vibrato, falsetto, belting, scat, portamento, rap, ad libs, riffs. Use them.

**Sacred or secular, and in what language?** Latin usually points to church music, especially before about 1600; a vernacular language points to the Reformation onwards, or to any secular tradition.

**And remember the studio.** Since the 1960s a vocal can be double tracked, layered into harmony by one singer, or corrected in pitch. That is part of the sonority.
examinerErrors: Writing "a woman singing" or "a high voice" where a voice type was wanted.
Assuming any high voice is female, when a countertenor is a high male voice.
Claiming word painting without quoting the word being painted.
Calling a verse-and-chorus song strophic, when the two are different shapes.
Describing the singing rather than the music: "she has a lovely voice".
Ignoring the accompaniment, which is half the texture.
Missing the studio in a popular song, where some of what is heard was never sung live.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer names the voice type and says what it is doing, then describes the word setting by counting rather than by impression. It quotes the word whenever it claims word painting. It knows that strophic and verse-and-chorus are different shapes and can say which it is hearing and why. It treats the accompaniment as part of the music rather than as background, and in a popular song it treats the studio as part of the sonority. And it uses the vocabulary of the right tradition: melisma and word painting for Purcell, multi-tracking and overdubbing for Queen.
